reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its stated purpose is to call and document a purported scammer, presenting the recordings as evidence rather than offering the caller's service. The remote-access instructions, affiliation claim, browser warning, and paid support plans are attributed to the caller or depicted computer interaction. The creator challenges the caller and questions the caller's website response, making these risk indicators subject matter of a critical investigation rather than creator solicitation or endorsement.

opening.argument: The video presents a concrete paid computer-protection offer tied to specific viewer actions. The caller instructs the user to install anti-hacking tools, promises complete protection, and asks the user to select a service term. The offer then moves directly to payment: the caller quotes six-month and one-year prices, adds two-year and lifetime plans, and says a billing department will call after the computer is cleaned. That is a recognizable solicitation sequence: authorize access, choose a protection package, and proceed to billing in exchange for promised security and cleanup.

you can protect your computer completely and no one can touch your computer in the world without your permission, okay?
If you go for a six month, it's just $99. If you go for a year, it's just $149.
I'll clean up everything from your computer and our billing department will call you back

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the interaction an investigation does not erase the commercial mechanism shown. The recording still contains a paid protection offer, term selection, and promised cleanup followed by a billing call. The creator's commentary may criticize the caller, but the observable sequence remains a service solicitation directed through remote access and payment.

citations.quote: Which one would you like to go for it? It's for six months or a year or two years or a lifetime.
our billing department will call you back

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The paid offer is spoken by the person on the support call, not endorsed by the video's creator. The surrounding commentary identifies the purpose as calling a scammer and recording evidence, while the creator directly challenges the caller's conduct. Those facts show the service pitch is the subject being documented, not an offer viewers are being asked to purchase.

citations.quote: in today's video We call another scammer of course.
I make these videos for evidence, you know, things like that.
Why do you guys like scamming people so much?

opening.argument: The evidence combines several high-pressure risk signals into one pathway. The on-screen alert says the computer has been blocked and repeatedly directs the user to call immediately, while warning that sensitive information may be stolen. The caller then uses remote-control software, claims the computer has corrupted files, and displays a large error count before offering paid protection. The combination of an urgent security warning, alleged data exposure, remote access, and a paid remedy is materially more concerning than any isolated technical-support statement.

citations.quote: Which are already corrupted by the hacker, can I go ahead and do that?

rebuttal.rebuttal: The supposed warning is not merely background scenery: it is paired with repeated instructions to call and with remote-control credentials visible in the same sequence. The caller also converts the displayed errors into a claim of hacking and then offers paid protection. Even if individual elements could have benign explanations, their combination creates the pressure structure that matters.

citations.quote: I can go ahead and install anti-hacking tools to your computer, okay?

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The frames and dialogue are presented as material being examined, not as claims made by the creator. The caller is the one who says the files were corrupted by a hacker and proposes the protection service. The creator instead asks whether the caller is affiliated with Microsoft and questions why the caller scams people, which makes the red flags the target of scrutiny.

citations.quote: you're currently connected to United Technical Department, sir. We work under Microsoft and Google, okay?
Why do you guys like scamming people so much?
I make these videos for evidence, you know, things like that.

opening.argument: Despite its investigative framing, the video makes the purported service easy to identify and inspect. The title prominently supplies both the service name and a phone number, the description lists a website and additional contact information, and the creator explicitly tells viewers they will enjoy looking at and checking out the website. That gives viewers a destination and contact path, while the extended call demonstrates how the service operates. The result can function as exposure and traffic generation for the very operation it claims to criticize.

citations.quote: TECH SUPPORT SCAMMER WORKS FOR GOOGLE!? "bestpccare" | [PHONE] | bestpccare.info
Scammer info: Number: 18448709810 Code: 2 943 455 Website: bestpccare.info
Everyone that watches this video will enjoy looking at it and, you know, checking it out.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The distribution choices still matter: the title, description, and spoken commentary provide identifiable contact destinations, and the creator expressly discusses viewers checking the website. Calling the material evidence does not prevent those details from increasing discoverability or directing attention toward the service.

Website: bestpccare.info
checking it out

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The contact details are supplied as identifying information about the purported scammer, not as a recommendation. The same speaker asks why the operators scam people and says the videos are made for evidence. The reference to viewers checking the site is embedded in sarcastic criticism after challenging the caller, so it does not establish endorsement or a request to buy anything.
